verdicts.text: Among dedicated IaC tools, Terraform is the most-starred, followed by OpenTofu, Pulumi, AWS CDK, and Crossplane; Kubernetes leads the broader ecosystem by GitHub stars.
verdicts.evidence: An independent September 2026 source gives the stars as "Terraform sits around 49,700 stars, OpenTofu around 30,200, Pulumi around 25,700, and Crossplane on GitHub shows around 12,100". GitHub's aws/aws-cdk page shows "Star 12.9k", which puts AWS CDK just ahead of Crossplane (~12.1k), so the order Terraform > OpenTofu > Pulumi > AWS CDK > Crossplane holds. Kubernetes (~128k) is well ahead of all of them.
verdicts.framing_note: This is a ranking claim, and independent star counts from Sept 2026 back up the order. The Kubernetes lead is supported only by the Pulumi blog itself (~127.9k) and general knowledge, not by an independent fetched source.
verdicts.intuition_flag: AWS CDK (~12.9k) and Crossplane (~12.1k) are only ~800 stars apart, so their order could flip over time.

verdicts.text: Cloud-native tools like AWS CDK, CloudFormation, Azure ARM, Azure Bicep, and Google Cloud Infrastructure Manager carry no separate tool fee; open-source tools OpenTofu, Kubernetes, and Crossplane are free to run.
verdicts.evidence: Google's Infrastructure Manager pricing page lists no fee for the service itself: "Infrastructure Manager charges for Cloud Build execution and Cloud Storage storage." So the claim of "no separate tool fee" holds, since you pay only for the underlying services. The rest matches common knowledge: CDK, ARM and Bicep have no fee, and OpenTofu, Kubernetes and Crossplane are open source.
verdicts.framing_note: Caveats: Infrastructure Manager bills for the Cloud Build minutes and Cloud Storage it uses, and CloudFormation charges per handler operation for third-party resource types or hooks. Neither is a tool fee for native use.
verdicts.intuition_flag: Kubernetes is grouped with IaC tools here, and "free" leaves out the cost of the underlying services (Cloud Build, and CloudFormation's third-party extensions).

verdicts.text: HCP Terraform is free for up to 500 managed resources with one concurrent run, then per-resource pricing of roughly $0.10 to $0.99 per resource per month depending on tier; self-hosted Terraform Enterprise is custom priced.
verdicts.evidence: Several 2026 third-party pricing write-ups agree with every part of the claim. Scalr (Sept 2026) says: "an enhanced free tier continues at up to 500 managed resources and one concurrent run." Paid tiers are Essentials $0.10, Standard $0.47 and Premium $0.99 per resource per month. Terraform Enterprise is "the self-hosted offering with custom pricing."
verdicts.framing_note: No source is cited in the claim. The evidence is secondary (competitor blogs dated June–Sept 2026), not HashiCorp's own pricing page.

verdicts.text: HCP Terraform is free for up to 500 managed resources with one concurrent run, then moves to per-resource pricing of roughly $0.10 to $0.99 per resource per month depending on tier.
verdicts.evidence: HashiCorp docs: "Free plan: No charge for up to 500 managed resources." Several 2026 third-party guides agree on 1 concurrent run for Free and list per-resource prices of $0.10 (Essentials), $0.47 (Standard) and $0.99 (Premium) per month, e.g. Spacelift: "The Free plan includes up to 500 managed resources and 1 concurrent run."
verdicts.framing_note: The HashiCorp page shown says only 500 free resources and points to its pricing page for rates. The per-tier dollar amounts and the 1-concurrent-run limit come from third-party guides dated Jul–Sep 2026, and they all agree.

verdicts.text: Self-hosted Terraform Enterprise is available at custom pricing.
verdicts.evidence: Several third-party pricing guides from 2025–2026 say self-hosted Terraform Enterprise is custom-priced. ControlMonkey: "The Terraform Enterprise self-hosted pricing is custom." env0: TFE "comes at a custom price." The HashiCorp pricing page snippet I found did not state this directly. Marketplace listings show reference prices starting around $15,000/year, but those are still negotiated offers.
verdicts.framing_note: Third-party sources say "custom pricing," which matches the claim. HashiCorp's own page wasn't quoted, so confidence is medium.

verdicts.text: Terraform's larger community reflects a decade of first-mover adoption.
verdicts.evidence: This is an editorial explanation of *why* Terraform has more stars (L1498). The cause it gives, first-mover adoption, is opinion and can't be tested against any source. The timing part fits: Terraform came out in 2014, so it has been around for about a decade. No Pulumi source or repo file addresses this.
verdicts.source: repo:content/blog/infrastructure-as-code-tools/index.md L1498 (context only; not used as evidence)
verdicts.intuition_flag: 'First-mover' is debatable. CloudFormation (2011), Chef and Puppet all came before Terraform, so it was only first among multi-cloud declarative IaC tools. Consider saying 'early-mover' or 'over a decade of adoption' instead.

verdicts.text: Kubernetes leads the broader infrastructure ecosystem by GitHub stars.
verdicts.evidence: The EvanLi Github-Ranking list (updated Sep 2026) shows kubernetes at 128,035 stars, ranked #4 among Go repos. Only awesome-go (a curated list), ollama (an LLM runner) and the Go language itself rank higher, and none of those is conventional infrastructure tooling. Terraform, Ansible and Docker/moby all have far fewer stars (tens of thousands), so Kubernetes plausibly leads infrastructure projects.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Broader infrastructure ecosystem" is vague. If AI serving tools like ollama (~182k stars) count as infrastructure, Kubernetes would not lead.
